newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Moody's sees big Australian bank mergers in future.
newsitem.headline: Moody's sees big Australian bank mergers in future.

text.p: U.S. credit rating agency Moody's Investors Service said on Tuesday it expected some of Australia's major banks to merge in response to a squeeze on lending margins and profitability.
The agency's Australian bank specialist, Sean Jones, said mergers among Australia's six independent banks would be seen, at worst, as a neutral move for bank creditors and depositors.

The remaining independent banks are National Australia Bank Ltd (NAB), Westpac Banking Corporation, Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd (ANZ), Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Adelaide Bank Ltd and Macquarie Bank Ltd, he said.
Competition from securitised home mortgage lenders in the Australian market had cut net interest margins from around five percent to about four percent or below for the four major banks.
"I would not be surprised if, in the second half of 1997, net interest margin falls well into the high threes," Jones told an investors' briefing in Melbourne.
This is pressuring the banks' cost structures, he added.
"It makes sense if these (the six banks) also consolidate and we would not be surprised if this did occur and we would see it as being neutral to positive...," Jones said.
Australia's "Big Four" banks are the NAB, the ANZ, Westpac and the Commonwealth.
Jones' comments come at a time when the market leader, NAB, wants a government ban on big bank mergers overturned.

But the government wants to see lending competition spread from home mortgages to small business loans before lifting the ban, as recommended in the recent official Wallis Report on the financial system.

Since the Reserve Bank of Australia cut official interest rates to 5.5 percent from six percent last Friday, only part of which was passed on by the banks, the government has virtually urged home borrowers to take their business to non-bank lenders.
But Jones said the unrelenting need to cut costs would eventually force the banks to consolidate further.
"There's a political hurdle but, regardless, we still see consolidation taking place," he said.
Later, he told reporters mergers were likely to mean "pretty sizeable" staff cuts and attacks on fixed-asset costs.
He declined to speculate on the likely extent of more mergers. "How it works out in the future, specifically, I cannot tell you," he said.
